**No-hair theorem**
States that a black hole that has settled into a stable state is completely described by just three externally observable properties: mass, electric charge, and angular momentum. All other information about the matter that formed it is hidden, so black holes "have no hair." This is the most common clue in black hole questions.

**Schwarzschild radius (2GM/c²)**
The radius of the event horizon of a non-rotating, uncharged black hole, equal to 2 times the gravitational constant G times the mass, divided by the speed of light squared. Any object compressed to a size smaller than its Schwarzschild radius collapses into a black hole. The Schwarzschild metric is the simplest black hole solution of Einstein's field equations, and Birkhoff's theorem shows it is the only spherically symmetric vacuum solution.

**Hawking radiation**
Thermal radiation that Stephen Hawking predicted black holes emit because of quantum effects near the event horizon, often pictured as particle-antiparticle pair production with one particle escaping. It causes black holes to slowly lose mass and "evaporate," shrinking their Schwarzschild radius. The evaporation time is proportional to the cube of the mass.

**Penrose process and the ergosphere**
The ergosphere is a region just outside the event horizon of a rotating black hole where spacetime is dragged so strongly that nothing can stay still. The Penrose process is a theoretical way to extract energy from it, which slows the black hole's rotation until it loses its angular momentum.

**Kerr metric and frame dragging**
The Kerr metric is the solution of Einstein's equations describing a rotating, uncharged black hole, which has mass and angular momentum. Rotating black holes drag spacetime around with them, an effect called frame dragging or the Lense-Thirring effect. A conserved quantity for orbits around them is the Carter constant.

**Reissner-Nordström and Kerr-Newman metrics**
The Reissner-Nordström metric describes a charged, non-rotating black hole, which has an inner Cauchy horizon as well as an outer event horizon. The Kerr-Newman metric is the general stationary solution for a black hole that is both charged and rotating.

**Supermassive black holes, Sagittarius A*, and quasars**
Most large galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their center, millions to billions of times the Sun's mass. The Milky Way's is Sagittarius A*. Matter falling into an accretion disk around such a black hole can power quasars and active galactic nuclei, and the black hole's mass can be measured by reverberation mapping.

**Event horizon and singularity**
The event horizon is the boundary inside which the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so nothing can get out. At the center lies a gravitational singularity, where density becomes infinite. The cosmic censorship hypothesis proposes that singularities are always hidden behind event horizons, so there are no "naked" singularities.

**Cygnus X-1 and X-ray binaries**
Cygnus X-1 is an X-ray binary, a black hole pulling material from a companion star, and it was the first object widely accepted as a black hole. Kip Thorne won a famous bet with Stephen Hawking over whether it was a black hole. Black holes are often detected through the X-rays given off by matter heated as it falls in.

**Bekenstein-Hawking entropy and the holographic principle**
Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that a black hole's entropy is proportional to the area of its event horizon, not its volume: it equals Boltzmann's constant times the area divided by four times the Planck length squared. This result helped inspire the holographic principle, the idea that a region's information can be encoded on its boundary.

**Black hole information paradox and the firewall**
Hawking radiation seems to destroy information about what fell into a black hole, which conflicts with quantum mechanics. In 2012 the AMPS group proposed a "firewall" of high-energy particles at the horizon as one resolution. Susskind and Maldacena proposed "ER = EPR," linking wormholes to entanglement, and in 2014 Hawking argued that black holes have only apparent horizons.

**Spaghettification**
The stretching and squeezing of an object falling toward a black hole caused by extreme tidal forces. The pull on the near end is much stronger than on the far end, stretching the object into a long thin shape.

**Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) limit**
The maximum mass a neutron star can have before neutron degeneracy pressure can no longer resist gravity. A collapsing stellar core above this limit becomes a black hole. It plays the same role for neutron stars that the Chandrasekhar limit plays for white dwarfs.

**Event Horizon Telescope and Katie Bouman**
The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes around the world through very-long-baseline interferometry to image black holes directly. It produced the first image of a black hole's shadow (M87*) in 2019, and later one of Sagittarius A*. Katie Bouman developed CHIRP, an imaging algorithm used in the collaboration.
